strengths: Rosokutai is correctly framed as a Road Traffic Act roadside strip on roads without a sidewalk, not a curb
FAQ and intro refuse the false universal 'no sidewalks in Japan'
Zone 30, school-route paint, and leftover width versus philosophy are directionally sound
verified: 路側帯 (rosokutai) is defined in the Road Traffic Act as a marked roadside strip, typically where there is no sidewalk
Vehicles keep left in Japan; pedestrians on roads without sidewalks are generally directed toward the right-hand edge (Road Traffic Act Art. 10), with exceptions
Zone 30 (30 km/h living-road zones) is a real municipal traffic-calming program
Building Standards Act Art. 42(2) (2項道路) concerns certain pre-existing sub-4 m streets and centerline setbacks on rebuild—not all residential roads
questionable: Residential streets 'often rely' on 20 km/h and 'suffer' 50 km/h as if those were the operative Japanese design pair
Article 42-2 presented as a general setback-road explanation for missing sidewalks
unsupported: 20 km/h and 50 km/h as the humane versus dangerous operating speeds of Japanese shared residential streets
needs_source: Typical 'four to six meters' width band—plausible for 生活道路, not a cited national statistic

issues.problem: The article number is only partly specified. 42(2) roads are a subset of narrow pre-standard lanes. Treating them as the typical no-sidewalk mechanism is legally incomplete and easy to over-read.
issues.suggestion: Hedge or drop the article number. Describe lot-by-lot rebuild setbacks as one process; state that many 4–6 m roads never had a curb for width/cost reasons alone.

issues.problem: Those figures are not established Japanese residential design speeds in the draft. Default unsigned limits, Zone 30, and actual driving speeds are different things.
issues.suggestion: Remove the numbers. Contrast slow local driving with arterial behavior without inventing km/h claims.

issues.location: FAQ — Should pedestrians walk on the right or left?
issues.problem: The answer hedges ('specific provisions') without stating the usual legal default (right-hand edge, facing traffic). Practice does vary, so a hedge is required—but the FAQ currently withholds the one accurate clause.
issues.suggestion: State the usual right-edge default, then hedge that people follow the clearer edge and school-route paint. Do not write a legal exam.
